title: Atlas
shortDescription: A ride-dispatch backend that matches riders to nearby drivers, and keeps matching correctly and fast even while part of the infrastructure is dying mid-request.
description:
A rider requesting a ride needs a fast, fair match to a driver, even when the system behind the match is actively failing. Atlas exists to prove that the match still happens, correctly and quickly, while a piece of the infrastructure dies mid-request.

Three independently deployable services talk over **gRPC**/Protocol Buffers: dispatch-service (orchestrator), pricing-service (pure calculator), and trip-service (system of record, its own **MySQL** schema), each containerized with **Docker**. Matching is **two-stage**: a grid-bucket index narrows the drivers, a per-request **quad-tree** ranks them, and a **lookahead score** on projected time-to-pickup lets a driver about to finish a nearby ride beat a farther idle one. Road distance comes from **OSRM**, falling back to haversine math on timeout.

Deployed to **Kubernetes** with **Prometheus** and **Grafana**, then chaos-tested by killing a live dispatch pod mid-ramp to **500 req/s** on a routing stub: **0.00%** of **101,249** requests failed via idempotent retry, with no duplicate trips. Ride requests carry a per-rider **Idempotency-Key** with a lease-based claim and fencing tokens, so 30 concurrent same-key requests create one trip. Explicit 2-second gRPC deadlines turn a dead dependency into a fast, clean error instead of an unbounded hang.
fact: Named after Atlas, the game where every place starts with the last letter of the one before.

title: Quantico
shortDescription: A quantitative research pipeline built so a "no" is believable: it tests whether past stock behavior predicts next week's moves, and shows why a null result is not a bug.
description:
Most trading backtests look better than they are because the test quietly sees the future. Quantico is built so that a "no" is believable: when a signal does not hold up, it says so, and it can show why the answer is not a bug. It uses paper money only.

A **Python** pipeline predicts 5-day returns for **20** US large-caps over 19 years of daily data, scored out-of-sample on **expanding walk-forward** folds with a purge gap. Five significance gates were frozen before the first scoring run, and six integrity tests, including **planted-signal recovery** and a shuffle control, prove the harness would catch a real signal. The baseline lands at **IC 0.006** and **t 0.53**: **no validated edge**.

A **C++17** execution simulator is called as a subprocess and checked bit-exact against a Python reference on **3,600** random orders. It runs about **2x** faster end to end at 200k synthetic orders, packing included. Comparing immediate, TWAP, and VWAP execution found no reliable ranking, because the 0.4-0.7 bps gaps sat inside 3.4 bps of cost-model uncertainty. A daily paper loop keeps replay and forward days apart and holds any edge claim behind a pre-registered 52-rebalance rule. A **91-test** pytest suite runs in GitHub Actions.

title: Narada
shortDescription: An agentic search pipeline that turns a topic into a table where every cell links to its source page with a verified quote, and re-searches to fill any gaps.
description:
Ever wonder where an AI's answer actually came from? Narada is built around that question. Ask it about any topic and every fact it hands back links straight to the page it came from, so you never have to take a summary on faith.

It runs as an **agentic pipeline** in Python/FastAPI: scrapes the web concurrently, uses **LLM extraction** to turn pages into structured entity data (reading **schema.org** data directly when a page already has it), dedupes across sources by fuzzy name match, and computes a **completeness score**. When cells are still empty it generates targeted follow-up searches, for up to **2 rounds**.

Every cell carries its source URL and a quote, enforced at the **Pydantic** model layer so an unsourced value cannot exist. Each quote is then checked against the page it cites, and cells that fail stay in the table flagged unverified. The LLM layer is a provider abstraction over a single **LiteLLM** integration, so any LiteLLM-supported LLM and **3 search providers** swap via env config, with per-step model overrides and automatic failover. API keys travel as per-request headers and are never stored. Covered by an **80-test** pytest suite.
fact: Named after Narada, the Hindu sage who carries news between worlds.

title: Donna
shortDescription: An AI executive assistant that books appointments, handles reschedules, and messages clients for service businesses through a multi-agent system.
description:
Every service business loses time and money to scheduling chaos: missed calls, double-bookings, clients who fall through the cracks because no one followed up. Donna sits between the business owner (a gym, studio, or consultant) and their clients, handling scheduling, reschedules, and client messages so the owner does not have to.

It is a **multi-agent system** in Python/FastAPI where each agent is an LLM tool-use loop: an orchestrator routes owner and client texts by phone number to **isolated per-client agents**, so no client's context bleeds into another's.

Every database write runs through typed **FastMCP** tools, with a runtime guard that raises on any bypass. A **two-stage LLM firewall** screens messages for prompt injection and identity spoofing and fails closed on scanner errors. A separate judge model checks each model-written reply against the turn's tool results before it is sent. Verified with a **101-test** pytest suite and **9 of 9** live scenarios on two local models. On a held-out hand-written set the firewall blocked **16 of 20** injections with **0 of 20** benign client messages falsely blocked.
fact: Inspired by Donna Paulsen from Suits, the assistant who is always a step ahead of what the business needs.

title: RiskWise
shortDescription: A maritime route risk scorer that computes a 0-100 score in code from live public events, then has an LLM agent pick reroutes that code computed and scored.
description:
Shipping companies commit to a route without a clear, real-time picture of what could go wrong along it. RiskWise gives them an honest, reproducible risk score and suggested alternatives before they commit, not after something breaks.

Give it a route and code computes a **0-100** score across **4 factors** (weather, labor, geopolitical, congestion) from live **NASA EONET**, **USGS**, and maritime news events near the route. The LLM never produces a number. When the score is high, a tool-using LLM agent picks among alternative lanes that code computed and scored, with a deterministic fallback if the model fails or names a route no tool returned. Alternatives are computed on a hand-built sea-lane graph, not AIS data.

Every stored disruption is labeled live, baseline, or LLM-generated, synthetic events stay out of scoring, and evaluations fail with a clear error instead of a made-up score when every live feed is down. The **4-page React dashboard** runs on **tRPC** end-to-end types and Drizzle/PostgreSQL, with a **MapLibre GL JS** map, a live threat feed, and per-route trend sparklines. Pinned by **213** Vitest tests.

title: Clinical Copilot
shortDescription: A multi-agent clinical chart analyzer that turns raw patient notes into a SOAP note, red flags, a medication check, and a timeline.
description:
A clinician reviewing a new patient's notes has to manually rebuild the chart context every time: what medications, what red flags, what timeline. Clinical Copilot builds that chart in seconds instead of an afternoon, and still produces something usable even if the AI call fails.

A **6-agent pipeline** in Python/FastAPI turns uploaded notes (PDF, DOCX, TXT, MD) into a SOAP note, red-flag list, medication reconciliation, and timeline. Every agent pairs **deterministic clinical rules** with LLM extraction, so output survives an LLM failure. **Medication and timeline agents run in parallel** ahead of risk and synthesis.

Medication data is enriched through the **OpenFDA drug label API** for interaction alerts, with a 4s timeout so slow lookups never block. A single run produces two reports from the same data: a clinician-facing version and a plain-language patient-facing one. All LLM calls route through a **LiteLLM** gateway. The live demo on Render takes visitors' own LLM provider key, held in sessionStorage and never logged or persisted.
fact: Built with two friends at an MIT hackathon run by SundAI and Weights & Biases.

title: Heimdall
shortDescription: An AI agent that triages B2B wholesale inquiries, checking customer, stock, and production cost before handing a human a draft to review and approve.
description:
A wholesale inquiry ("I want 500 units, what's your pricing?") looks simple but hides real judgment: is this buyer legitimate, can the order ship from current stock, what does a shortfall cost in time and money. Heimdall does that judgment automatically and hands a human a draft to approve, never a message that goes out on its own.

It is a **Gemini ADK agent** (Google Agent Development Kit) that checks customer, stock, and production cost over **read-only MCP tools** on stdio, then drafts a reply held for human approval. The shortfall logic (DTC velocity plus wholesale ask, minus stock) routes to a production-cost estimate only when stock falls short.

Input and output firewalls run as model callbacks. A **before-model callback** redacts **PII** and blocks prompt injection, including zero-width and Unicode evasion, before the LLM sees the input. An **after-model callback** re-scans the draft for leaked PII and language implying an auto-sent action. Because every tool is read-only, there is no write path and no code path to an auto-sent message.
fact: Named after the Norse watchman of the gods who guards the Bifröst bridge, played by Idris Elba in the Thor films.

title: Deepfake Deconstruction
shortDescription: A deep learning pipeline that traces a face-swapped image back to the original source photo it was built from, instead of just flagging that it's fake.
description:
Most deepfake detection stops at "this is fake," which tells you nothing about where the manipulation actually came from. This project goes a step further: given a face-swapped image, it traces it back to the real source photo.

A **modular PyTorch pipeline** uses **CNN** feature-extraction modules that can be swapped one at a time, so upgrading a single module never forces a pipeline rewrite.

It reaches **85%+ source-identification accuracy** on a custom dataset of **10,000+** manipulated images. The task is framed as source attribution instead of binary fake/real detection.

title: Stroke Biomarker Extraction
shortDescription: An ML pipeline that predicts stroke-recovery clinical scores from wrist-accelerometer data and measures which parts of a pretrained movement model's output can be trusted.
description:
Wrist trackers are cheap and always worn, so if the movement signal they capture carries a real clinical signal, stroke recovery could be monitored without a clinic visit. This project measures how much of that signal a pretrained movement model actually captures, and which parts of its output are reliable enough to trust.

Raw wrist-accelerometer recordings (**587,046** windows from **61** subjects) are preprocessed into per-visit files and run through a frozen pretrained transformer into **1028-d embeddings**. The pretrained model was provided by the course and never trained or fine-tuned by the team.

**Leave-one-subject-out** ablations show the **128-d accelerometer stream alone** beats the full 1028-d embedding on ARAT (R2 approx 0.49 to 0.56) and FMA (approx 0.41 to 0.48), while the 900-d gravity stream is noise. Engineered movement biomarkers on top of the frozen embeddings, validated for reliability and responsiveness, reach ARAT R2 approx 0.61 with the top 100 Spearman-selected features. A graduate course team project (CS690R, UMass Amherst).

title: DKeeper
shortDescription: A note-taking app on the Internet Computer, with a React frontend calling a Motoko canister directly and no REST API or database.
description:
Most apps assume a server is always there. DKeeper explores the alternative: a note-taking app whose backend is a canister on the Internet Computer rather than a server and a database.

A **React** and **TypeScript** frontend calls a **Motoko** canister directly through generated **Candid** bindings, with no REST API or backend server in between. Notes persist in canister stable variables with canister-assigned IDs, so data survives upgrades with no database.

TypeScript types are generated straight from the canister's typed Candid interface, so client and canister cannot drift apart. It runs locally and is deliberately scoped small, with no authentication.
